extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and constitutional design; policymakers interested in forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying evaluative criteria for constitutional design and assessing forms of government (mixed vs. simple democracies, aristocracies, monarchies), including electoral rules, faction-management, accountability, and institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of more than one branch of power
rubrics_metrics.description: “the necessity of more than one branch of power... The single struggle for the first place must eternally distract every simple government”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that single assemblies (one- or two-branch systems) inevitably create permanent contention for precedence; a legal, constitutional, and habitual mode of determining who shall be foremost is required to secure tranquillity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple balance of equal powers to check factions
rubrics_metrics.description: “a triple balance of equal powers affords a never-failing remedy against either”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A three-part balance (three branches) is advanced as the reliable safeguard against factional dominance; historical examples are cited where factions or family powers destroyed states (Rome, Carthage, etc.) to motivate this design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design government so mixed that factions may always be ruled
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is amazing that all that have happened, have not been sufficient to shew the necessity of a government so mixed that factions may always be ruled.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should explicitly provide mechanisms to control factions of the one, the few, or the many; without such mixture, particular species of faction can arise for which the constitution affords no defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational electoral methods and effectual anti-corruption provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: “some more rational method of determining the people's votes in elections, and some effectual provision against corruption.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral systems must reduce influences of family fortune, superstition, prejudice, name, and whim; the electorate should be taught to be governed more by reason and less by sounds (titles), and practical anti-corruption safeguards are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent wealth-based barriers to public service
rubrics_metrics.description: “No man can serve them who is not rich; this is giving up their own right of election into the hands of an aristocracy”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutional expectations that service be unpaid or that only the rich can serve, since that hands elections to an aristocracy and imports inequitable wealth-based selection and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic education and moral/scientific improvement of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: “To improve this, morals and science must be improved, extended, and made more general”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term constitutional success depends on raising public virtue and understanding; without broader education and moral improvement the electorate will remain susceptible to chicanery and poor choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow prudential continuation for executive/secrets of state with accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between acta imperii (laws) and arcana imperii (secrets of state): “secrets of state... require prudence, time, and experience... a prudential continuation of these may (without question) and ought to be, allowed... because if they do amiss, they are easily accountable to the people's assemblies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve executive/secret functions to experienced hands with some continuity while ensuring they remain accountable to representative assemblies to prevent maladministration; acknowledges trade-off with risk of standing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against standing powers and appointment-based corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “they will be the friends and confidents of the prevailing party... standing power... the whole executive and judicial power, and all the public treasure, is at once applied to corrupt the legislature and its electors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design appointment, reward, impeachment, and pay mechanisms so that leaders cannot capture instruments of government (treasury, appointments, judicial office) to corrupt the legislature or manipulate elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude disloyal or dangerous elements during revolutionary or unstable periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Author excludes certain parties (e.g., royalists) from voting or being chosen in times of danger: “he therefore excludes them from voting, or being chosen, and justifies it by Greek and Roman examples.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary exclusions of groups seen as a source of confusion or counter-revolution may be justified by some writers during unstable transitions; applicability depends on time and circumstances and raises normative concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government as the best design to prevent, manage, and remedy tumults
rubrics_metrics.description: “A mixed government, of all others, is best calculated to prevent, to manage, and to remedy tumults, by doing justice to all men on all occasions, to the minority as well as majority.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tumults arise from privileges, leader misconduct, and perceived oppression; a balanced constitution should enable impartial justice and channels for redress to reduce the frequency and harm of tumults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide institutional mechanisms to prosecute high crimes and punish calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: “In a mixed government... The grand inquest of the nation becomes accuser against those in high places... Calumny itself is punishable as an offence against the public.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish public legal processes (e.g., grand inquest, county inquests) to hold high officials to account and criminalize malicious false accusation, balancing public safety with protection from private-motive informers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect minorities from the tyranny of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the assertion that majority may 'make slaves of the minority' and warning that sovereignty absolutized would end the rights of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must include safeguards (legal protections, checks and balances) to prevent majorities from permanently dispossessing or oppressing minorities; majority rule must be constrained by rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate clearly between laws (public grievances) and executive secrets (state affairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: “By acts of state he means the laws and ordinances of the legislative power... Matters of grievance being matters of common sense... But as to secrets of state, or the executive part... these things being of a nature remote from ordinary apprehensions, and such as necessarily require prudence, time, and experience...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures should handle obvious public grievances through laws accessible to common understanding, while the executive should manage arcana imperii with appropriate expertise and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular returns and fixed periods of succession for assemblies as a remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Athens upheld constant returns and periods of succession in their supreme assemblies for remedy of grievances; and they had a standing council... to whom the secrets of state were committed... and variedly continued or excluded, as the people found cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic rotation and fixed terms for representatives, combined with accountable standing councils for continuity, can help remedy grievances while preventing accumulation of permanent personal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit unlimited liberty of accusation in simple democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: “In a simple democracy it would be unlimited; every body belonging to the majority would be informers and accusers... always sure of supporting his accusation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unfettered accusation by a majority can produce perpetual calumny and lawlessness; constitutional arrangements should channel accusations through public institutions and legal standards to avoid mass abuse.
